lead: FM gives its large noise improvement only while the received carrier is well above the noise. When the carrier-to-noise ratio in the IF bandwidth falls to about 10 dB, the output starts to crackle with clicks and the output SNR drops far faster than the ideal law. This is the threshold effect. The same nonlinear behaviour of the limiter and discriminator gives the capture effect: of two FM signals on one channel, the stronger takes over the output once it exceeds the weaker by the capture ratio, and the weaker is largely suppressed. Threshold and capture decide FM coverage and how closely channels can be reused.
prereq: You need: the FM figure of merit (see Noise in AM and FM receivers).

blocks.text: Measure the received carrier against the noise in the IF bandwidth B<sub>T</sub>: the carrier-to-noise ratio ρ = C/(N<sub>0</sub>B<sub>T</sub>). (The channel SNR of the figure-of-merit chapter measures the noise in W instead, so it is larger by B<sub>T</sub>/W.) Above threshold the output SNR follows a straight line: every extra dB of ρ gives one extra dB out, plus a fixed FM improvement.

blocks.where: ρ = C/(N<sub>0</sub>B<sub>T</sub>) is the carrier-to-noise ratio in B<sub>T</sub> = 2(β + 1)W; for β = 5 the factor 3β²(β + 1) = 450, a 26.5 dB improvement.

blocks.text: This is the (3/2)β² of the figure of merit rewritten with the noise in B<sub>T</sub>. It assumes the carrier phasor is much longer than the noise phasor, so the noise only tilts it a little. When the noise is nearly as large as the carrier, now and then it swings the resultant phasor right round the origin. The phase jumps by 2π in a moment, and the discriminator, which differentiates the phase, gives a sharp spike: a click. Clicks carry large power, so the output SNR collapses.

The threshold is usually defined as the ρ at which the output SNR is 1 dB below the straight line. For a tone with moderate β it lies near ρ = 10 dB; some books use 13 dB (ρ = 20) as the onset of clicks. Because B<sub>T</sub> grows with β, the carrier power at threshold grows too: in channel-SNR terms the threshold is about 20(β + 1) for ρ = 10. Wider deviation gives a better output above threshold but needs a stronger carrier to reach it.

sections.h3: The two-region picture and threshold extension

blocks.text: Figure 3.6.1 draws the straight-line law for the two receivers of the worked examples against received carrier power. Each line starts at its threshold point; below it, the dashed arrows only show that the output falls steeply, since the straight-line law no longer gives values there.

Threshold extension moves the knee to a lower ρ. An FM feedback (FMFB) receiver feeds the demodulated output back to its local oscillator, so the IF sees a compressed deviation and can use a narrower filter, letting in less noise. A phase-locked loop (PLL) detector tracks the carrier phase with a narrow loop and produces fewer clicks. Both trade circuit complexity for a few dB of threshold; few syllabi ask for more than the names, the aim and a block diagram.

When two FM signals share a channel, the limiter sees their sum. The resultant phasor follows the stronger one, and the weaker only wobbles its phase a little; after the discriminator the weaker programme is pushed far down. The capture ratio is the smallest power ratio, in dB, of the stronger to the weaker signal at which the receiver follows the stronger cleanly. Good broadcast receivers have capture ratios of a few dB.

This helps FM broadcasting: a distant co-channel station is weaker at your receiver, so it is captured out, with far less co-channel interference than AM would suffer. It also helped analog cellular reuse: the same channel could be used again in a cell far enough away for the wanted base station to exceed the interferer by the capture ratio. The catch: if the interferer becomes stronger, for instance as a car drives between two stations, the receiver suddenly switches to it. Capture ratio is a two-signal specification; threshold is a signal-to-noise specification.

examples.question: An FM broadcast receiver has an IF bandwidth B<sub>T</sub> = 180 kHz (β = 5, W = 15 kHz) and receives noise N<sub>0</sub> = kT<sub>0</sub> = 4 × 10⁻²¹ W/Hz. Taking the threshold as ρ = 10 dB, find the noise power, the carrier power at threshold, and the output SNR there.
steps: Output SNR at threshold = 10 + 26.5 = 36.5 dB. In channel-SNR terms, (S/N)<sub>c</sub> = 12ρ = 120 = 20.8 dB, and 20.8 + 15.7 (the FOM in dB) gives the same 36.5 dB.
examples.answer: N = 7.2 × 10⁻¹⁶ W (−121.4 dBm); C at threshold = 7.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ W (−111.4 dBm); output SNR there 36.5 dB.

examples.question: Compare the receiver of worked example 1 with one using β = 2 for the same 15 kHz audio and the same noise. Find the β = 2 bandwidth, threshold power and output SNR at threshold, and the output of each receiver at −111.4 dBm and at −114.4 dBm.
steps: Threshold C = 3.6 × 10⁻¹⁵ W = −114.4 dBm, 3 dB less than for β = 5.
Improvement 3 × 4 × 3 = 36 = 15.6 dB, so the output at threshold is 10 + 15.6 = 25.6 dB.
At −111.4 dBm: β = 5 is at threshold, 36.5 dB; β = 2 has ρ = 13.0 dB and gives 13.0 + 15.6 = 28.6 dB. Wide deviation wins by 8.0 dB.
At −114.4 dBm: β = 2 is at threshold, 25.6 dB; β = 5 has ρ = 7.0 dB, below threshold, and its output is full of clicks. Narrow deviation wins.
examples.answer: β = 2 needs 90 kHz and reaches threshold at −114.4 dBm with 25.6 dB out; at −111.4 dBm β = 5 gives 36.5 dB against 28.6 dB, but at −114.4 dBm only β = 2 still works.

traps: The threshold is a carrier-to-noise ratio of about 10 dB in the IF bandwidth; do not quote it as an output SNR or as a fixed power in watts.
Below threshold the straight-line law does not hold; do not use (S/N)<sub>o</sub> = 3β²(β + 1)ρ there.
Capture ratio is not threshold. Capture compares two signal powers; threshold compares carrier with noise.
A larger β improves the output above threshold but raises the carrier power needed to reach threshold (worked example 2).
Keep the two SNR measures apart: ρ uses the noise in B<sub>T</sub>, the channel SNR uses the noise in W; they differ by B<sub>T</sub>/W = 2(β + 1).

quiz.a: The carrier-to-noise ratio in the IF bandwidth at which the output SNR falls 1 dB below the above-threshold straight line; about 10 dB for usual receivers.

quiz.q: Why does the output SNR fall faster than the input below threshold?
quiz.a: The noise phasor is now sometimes larger than the carrier and swings the resultant round the origin. Each 2π phase jump gives a click at the discriminator output; clicks carry large power, so the output SNR collapses.

quiz.q: Above threshold a receiver gives (S/N)<sub>o</sub> = ρ + 14 dB. Find the output for ρ = 24 dB. Can you use the formula at ρ = 8 dB?
quiz.a: At 24 dB: 24 + 14 = 38 dB. At 8 dB the carrier is below threshold, so the formula does not hold and the actual output is much lower.

quiz.q: Two co-channel FM signals arrive at −70 dBm and −75 dBm. The capture ratio is 3 dB. Which does the receiver follow?
quiz.a: The difference is 5 dB, more than 3 dB, so the receiver follows the −70 dBm signal and largely suppresses the other.

quiz.q: Why is the capture effect useful for FM broadcasting and channel reuse, and what is its catch?
quiz.a: A weaker co-channel station is suppressed, so the same channel can be used again where the wanted signal exceeds the interferer by the capture ratio. The catch: if the interferer becomes the stronger, the receiver jumps to it.

quiz.q: Is capture ratio the same as threshold? Explain.
quiz.a: No. Threshold is a carrier-to-noise ratio for a 1 dB drop below the ideal law. Capture ratio is the power ratio of two co-channel signals needed for the stronger to take over.

quiz.q: An FM IF bandwidth is 200 kHz and N<sub>0</sub> = 4 × 10⁻²¹ W/Hz. Find the noise power and the carrier power at a 10 dB threshold.

beyond: Not for the exam. Threshold extension mattered most in early satellite and deep-space links, where every dB of carrier power was expensive. Click analysis, due to S. O. Rice, is still used to predict outages of FM links. Digital receivers meet the same problem as cycle slips in phase-locked loops. Search for FM threshold extension, FMFB and click noise.
